info.title: Internet Port Scan #1
info.subtitle: 64,790,266 Open Ports from April 2021
info.description:
### Content

64,790,266 open ports from 43,050,668 IP addresses, port scanned using [Masscan ](https://github.com/robertdavidgraham/masscan)between April 26, 2021 - April 30, 2021. Eleven ports were targeted.

| Port Number | Service |
| --- | --- |
| 21 | FTP |
| 22 | SSH |
| 23 | Telnet |
| 80 | HTTP |
| 443| HTTPS|
| 3389 | Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) |
| 4444 | Metasploit default listener |
| 5601 | Kibana |
| 8000| HTTP Alternate |
| 8443 | HTTPS Alternate |
| 9200 | Elasticsearch database |

### Notes

The Masscan tool is made to be fast and not accurate.

Cybersecurity researchers will want to use a slower but more accurate tool like [nmap](https://nmap.org/) to verify if a port is still open and perform additional scanning to see if there is truly an interesting service running on a port. For example, the [nmap script "http-title"](https://nmap.org/nsedoc/scripts/http-title.html) can be used to retrieve web page titles, which you can use to filter out pages you are not interested in.

This scan was targeted at 0.0.0.0/0 (the entire IPv4 address space) minus the IP ranges found in [Masscan's default exclusion file](https://github.com/robertdavidgraham/masscan/blob/master/data/exclude.conf). This removed private IP ranges and ranges belonging to various organizations who have complained about Masscan in the past.

[There are about 3,706,452,992 public IPv4 addresses](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/2437169/what-is-the-total-amount-of-public-ipv4-addresses) and this scan found open ports on only about 1% of them. It is safe to say this is not a complete, comprehensive, or accurate scan, due to the possibility of issues with the scan's configuration, host machine performance, etc.

This scan was launched from a e2-standard-2 (2 vCPUs, 8 GB memory) virtual machine running debian-10-buster-v20210420 in the us-east4-c zone of Google Cloud Platform. The Masscan rate was set to 500,000 packets per second but only achieved speeds of between 150,000 - 220,000 packets per second.

Some, if not the majority, of the ports found to be open belong to honeypots, proxies, and other devices that can report a port to be open although there is no "real" functioning service operating on that port. An easy way to test this is to scan an IP address with nmap. By default, nmap scans 1,000 of the most popular ports. If a target reports most of those ports to be open, it is probably a honeypot. Because this scan targeted only a few ports, it is not possible to tell if an IP is honeypot from this dataset alone.
